title: Isaac Newton
examples: What did Isaac Newton discover about falling objects?
Can you explain Newton's laws of motion simply?
How did Newton's work change science?

explain.say: Isaac Newton studied many important things in science.
He discovered that the Earth pulls objects towards its center.
Newton also described three laws about how things move.

items: Second Law: Force equals mass times acceleration
Third Law: Every action has an equal reaction

draw.text: Laws of Motion: Inertia, F=ma, Action-Reaction

explain.say: He made big discoveries about light and color too.

items: Spectrum emerges: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet

explain.say: Later, he developed calculus, a tool for change.
Think about riding a bicycle down a hill.

faq.a: Gravity is the force of attraction between any two objects that have mass. The more mass they have, the stronger the gravitational pull will be. It is sometimes called universal gravitation.
asks: What is the force pulling things down?

faq.q: Can you explain Newton's laws of motion simply?
faq.a: The first law says objects keep moving unless a force stops them. The second law relates force, mass, and acceleration. The third law states that forces come in equal and opposite pairs.
asks: What are the three laws Newton found?

faq.q: What did he discover about light?
faq.a: Newton used a prism to show that white light is actually made up of a spectrum of different colors. These colors bend at slightly different angles when passing through the prism.
Calculus is a branch of mathematics used to study continuous change. It helps us calculate things like the speed or the rate at which something is changing over time.
asks: What is the math of change?

faq.q: Did he discover gravity from an apple?
faq.a: The apple story is a popular tale, but it represents his thinking about why objects fall. He used it to develop the mathematical concept of universal gravitation.

facts: Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion.
He proposed that every object with mass pulls on every other object with mass.
Newton used prisms to demonstrate the spectrum of visible light.
Calculus is the mathematical study of continuous change.

quiz.say: If you push a toy car across a floor, and nothing stops it, what will it do?
quiz.show: The car will keep moving at a constant speed.

options.show: The car will keep moving at a constant speed.
options.say: The car will keep moving at a constant speed.

options.show: The car will speed up until it breaks.
options.say: The car will speed up until it breaks.

options.show: The car will curve into a circle.
options.say: The car will curve into a circle.

quiz.why: This matches Newton's first law, which states objects resist changes in motion.

wrong.1: This ignores the concept of inertia, which is the resistance to change.
wrong.2: Speeding up requires a continuous pushing or pulling force.
wrong.3: Curving requires a net force directed towards the center of the curve.

quiz.say: A book rests on a table. Which force is pulling the book down?
quiz.why: Gravity is the force exerted by the Earth pulling the book downwards.

wrong.0: The normal force is the table pushing up on the book, counteracting gravity.
wrong.2: Friction acts parallel to the surface, opposing motion, not pulling down.
wrong.3: Weight is the measurement of the force of gravity, not the name of the force itself.

quiz.say: If you throw a ball upwards, what happens when it reaches its highest point?
quiz.show: The ball momentarily stops before falling.

options.show: The upward and downward forces cancel out.
options.say: The upward and downward forces cancel out.

options.show: It will stop completely for a moment.
options.say: It will stop completely for a moment.

quiz.why: At the peak, the upward motion stops, but gravity immediately starts pulling it back down.

wrong.0: Unless thrown sideways, gravity only acts vertically downwards.
wrong.1: While the net force is zero instantaneously, the force of gravity is always present.
wrong.3: It stops momentarily, but 'completely' suggests no force acts on it.
